OF THE INDICATED PJM TRANSMISSION OWNERS

Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”) and the Commission’s Show Cause 
Order,2 the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners (“Indicated TOs”)3 submit this Motion for Leave 
to Answer and Answer to the various filings made in the above-captioned dockets on and after

because it ensures a further developed record for the Commission’s decision making.5 
I. The Standard Under Federal Power Act Section 206 Has Not Been Met. 
The Federal Power Act (“FPA”), under section 205, requires “[a]ll rates and charges made, 
demanded, or received by any public utility for or in connection with the transmission or sale of 
electric energy subject to the jurisdiction of the Commission, and all rules and regulations affecting 
or pertaining to such rates or charges shall be just and reasonable.”6  FPA section 206, on the other 
hand, empowers the Commission, on its own motion or upon complaint from a third party, to 
remedy any “rate [or] charge” or “any rule, regulation, practice, or contract affecting such rate [or] 
charge” that is found to be “unjust [or] unreasonable.”7  The requirement that the rate or charge 
must be found to be unjust and unreasonable before alternatives may be considered is a necessary, 
real, and meaningful one.  Only after a successful showing that the existing rate is unjust and 
unreasonable, may the Commission order a replacement rate.8  And, “[t]he burden of proving an 
unjust or unreasonable rate rests with the party that initiated the proceeding—that is, the 
Commission or the third-party complainant.”9  Neither the Commission nor any of the parties 
supporting the initiation of this FPA section 206 proceeding have demonstrated that the existing

PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff (“PJM Tariff”) is unjust and unreasonable.  Consequently, 
the only action that may lawfully be taken is to terminate this proceeding. 
A. The Current PJM Tariff Is Just and Reasonable and Not Unduly
Discriminatory, and No One Has Demonstrated Otherwise.
Notwithstanding proposed alternative arrangements for co-located load, no party has 
shown that the PJM Tariff is unjust and unreasonable.  Several parties have offered proposals that 
they claim would aid the development of co-located loads.  But, the Indicated TOs have explained 
at length why these proposals would harm, rather than help, the ability of PJM to accommodate 
co-located interconnection arrangements, and the attached Declaration of Danielle S. Powers 
(“Powers Declaration”) elaborates on those arguments.  More importantly, however, the claim—
even if it were true, which it is not—that a different tariff might advantage certain load does not 
demonstrate that the existing tariff is unjust or unreasonable.   
Some parties try to turn this process on its head.  They claim that the PJM Tariff should be 
changed because the Indicated TOs have not made an adequate “showing that PJM’s Tariff is just 
and reasonable or not unduly discriminatory, or that changes are not needed to enable progress.”10  
As the Indicated TOs have also repeatedly stressed, that is not the law; indeed, it is 180 degrees 
off.  The burden is not on PJM or the transmission owners to show that the PJM Tariff is just and 
reasonable; the burden is on parties seeking a change in the rate to demonstrate the existing tariff 
is not just and reasonable.  The Commission may order a replacement rate under Section 206 only 
after a successful showing that the prevailing rate is unjust and unreasonable.11  No such showing 
has been made.   
10  EPSA/P3 Comments at 3 (Apr. 23, 2025). 
11  16 U.S.C. § 824e(a); see also Pub. Citizen, Inc. v. FERC, 7 F.4th 1177, 1183 (D.C. Cir. 2021) (“The burden of 
proving an unjust or unreasonable rate rests with the party that initiated the proceeding—the Commission [(as in 
this case)] or the third-party complainant.”).

4 
 
Constellation argues that requiring all new load to become Network Load,12 like all other 
end use load, will cause “years of delay” and “induce[] massive and unnecessary overbuild of the 
system.”13  This claim is sensationalist and unsubstantiated.  No party has demonstrated that it has 
been unable to receive service under the existing system or that it is experiencing an undue delay 
for a request for service under the current PJM Tariff.  Nor has there been a coherent explanation 
for the claim that study processes of new large loads are unjust and unreasonable.  To the contrary, 
the evidence in the proceeding points to huge potential system impacts arising from contemplated 
city-sized loads, and a need for a reliability study regardless of how such loads propose to be 
connected.   
Nor does the fact that some parties are complaining about the PJM Tariff show that it is 
unjust or unreasonable.  There are two transmission options under the existing PJM Tariff: 
Network Integration Transmission Service (“Network Service” or “NITS”) or Point-to-Point 
Transmission Service (“PTP Service”).  A preference for alternative rate structures is not evidence 
that the existing forms of transmission service are unjust and unreasonable.  Vistra claims the 
existing PJM Tariff includes “a structural bias in favor of network transmission-serviced load and 
against competitive, bilateral supply arrangements between sophisticated buyers and market-based 
rate . . . sellers.”14  However, what Vistra wants is an alternative form of service that is cheaper for 
it at the expense of other transmission customers.  But the fact that the cheaper-for-Vistra (and 
other similarly situated entities) service is unavailable does not make the existing PJM Tariff 
unreasonable.  As explained above, there are options for customers to obtain service.  Those

13  Constellation Answer at 4 (Apr. 23, 2025). 
14  Vistra Comments at 4 (Apr. 23, 2025).

5 
 
options work and are provided at rates that the Commission has found to be just and reasonable 
and are designed to recover the embedded costs of the PJM grid.  There is nothing unjust or 
unreasonable about these well-established structures.  Moreover, the establishment of tariff 
provisions that would grant an advantage or preference in favor of co-located loads that would 
take but not pay for grid services—which is what is being attempted by some in this proceeding—
would result in a structural bias that benefits co-located load at the expense of other customers 
paying Network Service.  
Talen similarly argues that the PJM Tariff is unjust and unreasonable because it “do[es] 
not presently outline regulatory guardrails for many of the potential configurations that co-located 
load arrangements may take.”15  This argument amounts to nothing more than a desire for a 
cheaper option, without demonstrating why the existing service is unjust and unreasonable.  The 
necessary guardrails are the express service definitions.  No one has alleged that they cannot get 
service for their customers using existing transmission services.  Nothing in the FPA requires that 
a tariff provide alternative, more favorable treatment for co-located load.  In fact, such “regulatory 
guardrails” would flout the requirement in the FPA that a tariff not grant undue preference or undue 
rate discrimination among customers.16 
Beyond these untenable claims of harm, some parties’ arguments about the services to end-
use load connecting “behind” a generator’s meter rely on a single, flawed premise: that moving 
the location of the meter changes the degree to which a load relies on grid services or the nature 
of those services.  This is fiction.  So when Constellation claims that the Indicated TOs have 
“conflat[ed] the benefits received from ancillary services by the co-located generator with the use

of the transmission system to deliver energy,”17 or Vistra states that “transmission system charges 
for load served by co-located generation should be based on actual use of the transmission 
system,”18 they are pretending that the position of the generator’s meter actually changes those 
services.  It does not.  Nor does it change the fact that the generator and the load continue to rely 
on the grid connection to function.   
The Commission has rejected arguments that transmission service must be based on 
specific load flows because the “assessment of [Network Integration Transmission Service] is not 
based on actual use over a particular transmission path, but rather based on the network customer’s 
right to use the entire system.”19  This approach to transmission service also comports with FPA 
section 205(b), which prohibits an undue advantage or preference or “any unreasonable difference 
in rates, charges, service, facilities, or in any other respect . . . as between classes of service.”20  
And this is not the first time parties have attempted to argue for a new class of service.  In one such 
example, Amtrak v. PPL Electric Utilities Corp.,21 the complainant attempted to argue that it made 
lesser use of the grid and thus should be charged under some new arrangement that differed from 
the charges applicable to ordinary Network Service.  The Commission, however, rejected the 
complaint and found in accordance with the facts that the load was served by the PJM transmission 
system and thus was appropriately served through the Network Service applicable to Network 
Load.22

As demonstrated by the following diagram depicting an example configuration, moving 
the meter does not change grid usage: 
Parties supporting more favorable accommodations for co-located load under the PJM Tariff share 
one thing in common: their arguments are premised on the fiction that moving the location of the 
meter (from the example configuration at A and B to a new single meter at C) justifies a new form 
of service with a new rate construct.  In truth, moving placement of the meter does not change grid 
availability and support.  However, placement of load behind the meter can obscure load and hide 
information needed for system planning and grid operations.  It can result in obscured load that is 
not appropriately accounted for that can unpredictably move grid flows and voltages up and down, 
creating potentially dire circumstances if those variations were not planned for or accounted for 
by system operators.  Whether the meters are at C or at A and B, the grid operator and transmission 
owners must support and plan for both the load and the generator.

8 
 
Meter placement does not change the physics of the system—if the load suddenly increases 
or drops by 100 MW, the grid will experience that increase or decrease, no matter where the meter 
is located.  This is particularly true when the co-located unit is a nuclear plant as such plants cannot 
follow the load variations, so if there is an increase or decrease in load, it must be generators 
elsewhere on the grid that respond.  Regardless of whether a large load is behind the meter or in 
front of it, it impacts flows on the grid, and relies on grid services, and grid operators and 
transmission owners must therefore support and plan for it.  That does not justify a new form of 
service with a new rate construct.  The PJM Tariff in its current form allows the co-location of 
end-use load and generation on terms commensurate with cost-causation principles.23  And as the 
Indicated TOs have previously explained, “the mere presentation of potential options” does not 
render the existing PJM Tariff unjust and unreasonable.24  The PJM Tariff remains just and 
reasonable, so it cannot be changed as a result of this proceeding. 
When parties claim that the PJM Tariff is unjust and unreasonable in requiring Network 
Service because co-located load is “fully isolated” from the grid, they are using misleading 
nomenclature to misrepresent the physical reality.  As the Indicated TOs have explained 
previously, there is no such thing as a data center load configured to be “fully isolated” behind the 
meter through “system protection facilities,” because co-located load that is connected to the 
electric grid (a) necessarily relies on essential reliability services, such as ancillary services, 
including black start; (b) retains the potential to draw real or reactive power from the grid at any 
time; and (c) relies on and benefits from its connection to the transmission system at all times.25

24  Indicated TOs Answer at 9 (Apr. 23, 2025).

That generator and the end-use load also continue to rely on the transmission connection and 
investment to operate, just as if the load were “in front of the meter.”  Notably, PJM agrees that 
there is no such thing as “fully isolated” co-located load arrangement when there is a connection 
to the electric grid.26  Constellation is mistaken that a “protective relay scheme” will “prevent 
power flows from the PJM Transmission System . . . to the load,”27 and equally mistaken that the 
direction of real power flows is a sine qua non for use of, and reliance on, the transmission system.  
As explained by PJM, 
The notion that any of the proposed co-location arrangements can 
be “wholly isolated” is misleading. The load and generator are 
connected to and synchronized with the multi-state bulk power 
system.  It is not operating as a micro grid (nor can it if the 
generating facility is a nuclear unit).  Nor is the generator delivering 
power through an intermediary to a load with a breaker open.  
Further, by way of example, there are obligations to ensure power 
to nuclear plants to ensure safe shutdown (among other things).  The 
load and generator are benefiting from ancillary services (including 
but not limited to black start).  Any system protection facilities are 
designed to only handle less complex N-1 conditions, and can 
misoperate (and indeed have misoperated).28 
 
There is simply no guarantee that the relay systems and protection schemes will ensure that the 
reliability impacts of hidden load are mitigated or eliminated.  For example, the protection schemes 
appear to be largely focused on dealing with situations where the co-located generation unit has 
an outage, but the reliability concerns are not limited to a generation outage; even while the nuclear 
generator is producing its full output, there could be a reliability disaster due to rapid variations in

[in a question] as it is contrary to engineering and economic principles”); id. at 44 (“PJM is not aware of a 
configuration that would ‘ensure the co-located load never takes any form of transmission service.’”).

(Or to get back to the diagram, consider the situation where the meters are at A and B.  If the load 
at B has a relay installed so that it shuts off when the generator at A experiences an outage, that 
does not change the fact that the load at B impacts the grid second to second throughout the day.  
Putting a meter at C does not change that continual grid impact.) 
Further, requiring co-located loads to obtain Network Service is consistent with bedrock 
principles of Order Nos. 88830 and 200331 and the PJM Tariff.  It ensures that co-located load is 
properly accounted for in reliability planning and pays for its share of transmission and ancillary 
services from the grid.  Order No. 888 codifies the Commission’s decades-long endeavor of 
“Promoting Wholesale Competition Through Open Access Non-Discriminatory Transmission 
Services by Public Utilities.”32  It accomplishes this goal by requiring “all transmission-owning 
utilities to provide transmission service for electricity generated by others on the same basis that 
they provided transmission service of the electricity they themselves generated.”33  Consistent with 
this goal, co-located loads are—and should continue to be—treated like all other Network Load.

Contrary to some commenters’ assertions, this treatment of co-located load does not limit 
competition or stifle innovation.34  Instead, it places all load, co-located or not, on a level playing 
field where all customers pay for the transmission services that they receive.  It is not “anti-
competitive” to force everyone to play by the same rules.  Quite the opposite.  Classification as 
Network Load accounts for the physical reality that service to the co-located load requires 
Commission-jurisdictional services from the grid and should pay for those services in the same 
manner that all other load must pay. 
Several comments argue that co-location provides “benefits” to the grid, including 
reducing the need for new transmission infrastructure and improving reliability, and therefore co-
located load does not have to pay for its share of grid services.35  These unquantifiable benefits do 
nothing of the sort.  Similar benefits could be said to result from all types of load.  Indeed, as the 
Indicated TOs have previously explained, these benefits of efficient transmission planning and 
reliability are best served by treating co-located load as Network Load.36  Many loads are sited 
efficiently and could claim that their siting provides grid-wide benefits, but they still must pay 
their share of grid services because they rely on the grid for safe reliable service to keep the light 
on.  The current PJM Tariff enables just that.  Clarification from the Commission that co-located 
load is Network Load would further facilitate the benefits that these commenters emphasize.  They 
have failed to demonstrate that the way in which co-located load connects to the grid under the 
current PJM Tariff is unjust and unreasonable.  Treating co-located load in its current form under

35  E.g., PJMCC & IECA Comments at 12–13; ENGIE Comments at 6–7; Clean Air Task Force Comments at 12. 
36  Indicated TOs Answer at 7 (Apr. 23, 2025).

12 
 
the PJM Tariff (i.e., as Network Load) is essential for reliability, transmission planning, PJM’s 
procurement of adequate capacity, and appropriate cost allocation. 
What it comes down to is this: “[t]he reasonableness of a rate is assessed in light of the 
FPA’s goals of promoting reliable service at reasonable rates and developing plentiful energy 
supplies.”37  The existing PJM Tariff comports with those goals.  Rather than stymy transmission 
planning through allowing for load to be hidden from the transmission planning process and place 
the electric grid at risk, the existing PJM Tariff allows for effective planning, maintains reliability 
of the electric grid, provides transparent outcomes, and results in an even-handed approach to cost 
allocation.  Nothing in the FPA requires transmission operators to offer a service more favorable 
to co-location arrangements when there is a service that can already accommodate these 
arrangements (i.e., Network Service). 
Ultimately, the arguments presented by Talen, Vistra, and Constellation fail to demonstrate 
that the existing PJM Tariff is unjust or unreasonable. And while behind-the-meter generation 
arrangements have been “accommodat[ed]” in PJM for decades,38 as the Indicated TOs have 
previously explained and as further discussed below, behind-the-meter generation (“BTMG”) is 
not similarly situated to behind-the-meter co-located load.39  Different treatment of co-located load 
from BTMG, on account of the real differences between the two, is not unduly discriminatory.  
Accordingly, the existing PJM Tariff remains just and reasonable.

B. There Is No Basis to Change the Existing PJM Tariff to Accommodate Co-
located Load. 
 
Parties have lost sight of something throughout the course of this proceeding.  FERC cannot 
order a new type of service unless there is a finding that the existing arrangement is unlawful.  It 
is worth taking a moment to turn back to Order No. 888-A.  In that order, FERC stated the 
following: 
[T]here is no dispute that the FPA does not explicitly give this 
Commission authority to order, sua sponte, open access 
transmission services by public utilities.  However, the fact remains 
that the FPA does explicitly require this Commission to remedy 
undue discrimination by public utilities.  The finding of the D.C. 
Circuit in the AGD case, with regard to sections 4 and 5 of the NGA 
(which parallel sections 205 and 206 of the FPA), are equally 
applicable here: the Act “fairly bristles” with concerns regarding 
undue discrimination and it would turn statutory construction on its 
head to let the failure to grant a general power prevail over the 
affirmative grant of a specific one.40  
 
And the Supreme Court took note of this, stating that, “FERC acknowledged that it did not have 
the ‘authority to order, sua sponte, open-access transmission services by public utilities,’ but 
explained that § 206 of the FPA explicitly required it to remedy the undue discrimination that it 
had found.”41  This can be read to mean that, to the extent FERC required open access, FERC 
acknowledged that there was not express authority to do that without a finding that there was undue 
discrimination.  For FERC to require transmission service to accommodate certain loads, it would 
necessarily follow that FERC cannot order the creation of a new service under the PJM Tariff 
unless it makes a finding that the current treatment in the tariff constitutes undue discrimination.  
There is no basis to make that finding.  Under the existing PJM Tariff, Network Service is available

FERC action to the contrary would amount to an issue under the major questions doctrine. 
If Congress wanted to give FERC authority to order its preferred transmission service to benefit 
certain customers, it could have done so.42  It did not.  “Agencies have only those powers given to 
them by Congress, and ‘enabling legislation’ is generally not an ‘open book to which the agency 
[may] add pages and change the plot line.’”43  Not only does the Commission not have any 
authority to require a new type of transmission service to accommodate co-located load under the 
FPA, but any attempt by the Commission to set a replacement rate that would be a means to 
accommodate a narrow category of customers, such as co-located load, would run contrary to the 
declaration in the FPA that rates that provide an undue preference or advantage are unlawful. 
Specifically, FPA section 205(b) states that “[n]o public utility shall, with respect to any 
transmission or sale subject to the jurisdiction of the Commission, (1) make or grant any undue 
preference or advantage to any person or subject any person to any undue prejudice or

Finally, any suggestion the existing PJM Tariff is unduly discriminatory45 or preferential 
falls flat because the same service is offered to all customers and co-located loads can move 
forward using the existing PJM Tariff approach.   
II. There Is No Inconsistency in the Indicated TOs’ Jurisdictional Position. 
Talen asserts that “the Utilities have sought to extract two holdings from the Commission: 
(1) that co-located load always takes a form of FERC-jurisdictional transmission service and (2) 
that the interconnection of co-located load is not FERC jurisdictional.”46  Talen goes on to state 
that in “Exelon’s pending [petition for declaratory order] Proceeding (EL24-149), the Utilities 
have argued that the interconnection of end-use load is not FERC jurisdictional, supposedly 
because the interconnection procedures implemented by Order No. 2003 apply only to generation 
and not to load.”47  Talen then questions whether the utilities’ jurisdictional position is consistent 
within the various proceedings dealing with co-location.48  It is fully consistent.  It is the Network 
Service customer that is taking FERC-jurisdictional transmission service in serving the co-located 
load.  That is typically an LSE, but if a state allows, it may be the load itself.  The interconnection

the existing tariff. Finally, Mr. Ming ignores the fact that the primary 
motivation for large loads seeking co-location arrangements is not avoidance 
of transmission costs, but timely interconnection.  
9. Ultimately, the E3 Proposal ignores the fact that the current tariff already 
provides most of what E3 is seeking, other than the rate discounts which are 
unduly discriminatory against existing load as well as new load not included 
in the proposed favored class. Under the current tariff, loads that are capable 
of actually reducing demand at the time of the system peak can do so and 
thereby achieve a smaller peak coincident load and a lower allocation of costs 
as network customers. A discount for certain customers only is not justified 
under this framework and would be unduly discriminatory.

5 
III. 
E3’s Proposal Does Not Consider Reliability Concerns and Operational Impacts 
Addressed Through the Interconnection Process. 
A. Existing NERC Reliability Standards Ensure the Grid Can Reliably Serve the 
Full Requirement of the Load Under Both Normal and Contingency 
Conditions. 
10. TOs and Transmission Planners must determine the reliability impact of 
interconnecting new loads and generation in accordance with NERC 
Reliability Standards FAC-002-21 and TPL-001-5.2 TOs establish their own 
planning criteria and interconnection requirements in compliance with these 
NERC Reliability Standards. They assess the reliability impacts of the full-load 
requirement across a range of operating conditions. If a new load presents 
reliability concerns, the TO collaborates with the new load and the ISO to 
identify and implement appropriate mitigation measures.  
11. Allowing certain transmission customers with bundled load and generation to 
choose their own level of transmission service, especially outside of NITS, 
would represent a significant departure from these reliability standards. In 
fact, it would effectively bypass these requirements, introducing new and 
untested reliability risks. Without formal revisions to NERC’s Reliability 
Standards, TOs and ISOs are not authorized to operate under the parameters 
proposed by E3.  
12. The NERC Large Load Task Force is currently investigating the implications of 
large loads interconnecting to the Bulk Power System. This work includes 
 
1  
NERC Facilities Design, Connections, and Maintenance Reliability Standards. 
2  
NERC Transmission Planning Reliability Standards.

6 
evaluating whether and how forecasting, modeling, and interconnection 
processes could incorporate flexible demand profiles or on-site generation 
while still ensuring grid reliability. 
13. NERC’s study of these issues did not arise in a vacuum. There is growing 
experience with these new large loads and research into their power demand, 
and that experience and research suggest large and extreme system impacts. 
One regional operator, Electric Reliability Council of Texas (“ERCOT”), 
reported a 300 MW drop in data center demand in 24 seconds, and oscillations 
of 25 MW repeatedly up and down in under one second, recurring again with 
50 MW oscillations three days later.3   
14. It is not at all clear that the relay schemes and protection mechanisms that 
have been proposed by various large loads would protect the grid against such 
variations in data center demand. The protection schemes appear to be largely 
focused on dealing with situations where the co-located generation unit has 
an outage, but the above concerns do not relate to a generation outage and 
instead relate to rapid variations in demand. Given real concerns about 
extreme system impacts, adoption of a proposal to permit reduced scrutiny of 
large loads is contrary to the prioritization of reliability and system security. 
15. NERC has committed to developing a reliability guideline by June 2026 that 
will “identify risk mitigations and improvements to planning and operations 
 
3  
ERCOT Large Load Oscillation Event, LFLTF Meeting (stakeholder presentation) (Mar. 4, 2025), 
https://www.ercot.com/calendar/03042025-LFLTF-Meeting (choose “LL 
Oscillation_LFLTF_Mar2025_Final” link under “Key Documents”).

7 
for large loads interconnection requirements.”4 At the very least, until NERC’s 
assessment is complete, it is premature for FERC to approve proposals like 
E3’s that assume capabilities and standards that do not yet exist. 
B. E3’s Proposal Relies on a Flexible Bundled Interconnection Framework that 
Does Not Exist 
16. E3 mapped the eight co-located configurations proposed by PJM into three 
different co-location configurations: 
firm, generator-contingent, and 
interruptible. Both the generator-contingent and interruptible options assume 
that large loads can interconnect to the grid without the need for full 
transmission service, based on their ability to use large onsite generation or 
load shedding to offset consumption during peak conditions. For example, 
according to E3’s Proposal, if a 100-MW load can reduce its draw to 40 MW 
during the system peak by dispatching on-site generation or potentially by 
shedding a portion of its load, the grid should only be planned to serve the net 
40 MW load. This implies a flexible interconnection regime analogous to 
ERCOT’s “Connect and Manage” construct used for generation.  However, no 
such flexible interconnection framework currently exists for load nor for 
bundled load and generation anywhere in North America. 
17. In considering the interconnection study to be performed for the co-located 
generation and load, it is instructive to contemplate the circumstance where a 
new generator is proposed near a large load but not formally “co-located” with 
that large load.  For this example, consider an aluminum smelter, which is a 
 
4  
Comments of the North American Electric Reliability Corporation at 6 (Apr. 23, 2025).

8 
large electrical industrial load, and assume it is in a relatively import-
constrained area. In this example, the industrial load and the new generator 
are not co-located behind a meter point; they are physically adjacent but they 
are owned by different entities and have no contractual relationship. 
18. In evaluating the interconnection of this hypothetical new generator, the 
ISO/RTO and TO will recognize the import constraint as well as the industrial 
load, and the analysis will account for the fact that operation of this new 
generator will reduce congestion on the constraint. Because of this, the 
interconnection requirements will generally be minimal, aside from potential 
secondary issues such as short circuit duty or voltage control. The proposed 
generator would be required to fund transmission modifications to address 
these issues, a point conceded in the Ming testimony,5 but otherwise the 
interconnection requirements are likely to be significantly less than would be 
the case if it were interconnected outside the import constraint. 
19. Nothing changes from a reliability or electrical interconnection standpoint if 
this hypothetical new generator were to agree to formally co-locate with the 
industrial load inside the load pocket. The electrical and operational 
characteristics of the load and the generator are unchanged, the 
interconnection analysis must still account for the specific characteristics of 
each, and the interconnection requirement will be the same. The metering 
point makes no difference. Both the generator and the load do benefit from 
 
5  
See Answer of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC, at Ex. 2, Testimony of Zachery Ming, at 27:16–19 
(Apr. 23, 2025).

9 
physically locating close together, but nothing about the contractual 
arrangement between the parties changes the physics of the system. 
Therefore, the interconnection study, the required reinforcements, and the 
interconnection cost are all the same whether the generation and load are 
contractually co-located or not. 
20. Importantly, interconnection of large load customers falls under state 
jurisdiction because it involves the provision of retail electric service, which is 
not regulated by FERC. When a large load, such as a data center, seeks to 
interconnect to the electric grid, it does so as a retail customer of the local 
utility, like any other load. The interconnection process, applicable rates, and 
service classifications are governed by the state-approved retail tariff, which 
establishes the rights and obligations of both the customer and the utility. This 
includes determinations about interconnection requirements and whether 
special rate treatment, such as generator-contingent or interruptible service, 
is available. 
C. Many Types of Large Load Have Not, Cannot, or Will Not Sign Up for these 
Types of Contractual Co-location Arrangements. 
21. It is important to note that a substantial amount of large load has already been 
added to the PJM grid under the existing interconnection rules. These loads 
have been studied and planned as Network Loads. They are paying for 
transmission costs just like any other load that depends on the grid for electric 
service. Applying a different standard would be inconsistent and unfair to 
those who have followed the established process.

10 
22. While certain types of large loads—such as crypto mining operations—may 
offer meaningful load flexibility due to their ability to curtail or reduce 
consumption almost instantly with minimal operational impact, other large 
loads, such as data centers and industrial facilities, may face significant 
constraints that limit their flexibility. 
23. For example, a large load such as a data center arranged as a tenant facility, 
wherein a number of different tenants contract with the owner of the data 
center facility, would not necessarily have the same operational 
characteristics as a large data center owned and operated by a single entity. In 
a tenant facility, portions of the facility might be able to curtail rapidly, while 
others might not. The provision of retail service to locations with tenant 
arrangements that serve customers with varying operational needs is normal. 
FERC rules that assume that an entire facility can be used one way or another 
simply do not comport with this reality. 
24. Given that the majority of large loads entering the PJM footprint cannot be 
readily interrupted, these loads would not be suitable for generator-
contingent or interruptible service. However, the types of loads capable of 
rapidly curtailing operation already possess the ability to minimize 
transmission costs through closely monitoring system conditions and 
curtailing whenever the system approaches its expected coincident peak. 
Operating in this manner may significantly reduce transmission charges since 
transmission costs are allocated based on the load contribution to system 
coincident peaks.

11 
IV. 
Role of a “Marginal Cost Discount” in Embedded Cost Ratemaking  
25. E3 references rate design principles established by Bonbright, among which is 
the idea that rates should be non-discriminatory.6 At the same time, E3 
proposes the use of marginal-cost discounted rate design for a specific class of 
customers while other similar transmission service customers would be 
charged rates that would continue to be based on full embedded costs. The 
application of E3’s rate design concepts leads to inequitable treatment of 
customer classes that is unduly discriminatory. For example, E3’s proposed 
treatment of customers taking “generator-contingent” service includes the 
idea that these customers should benefit from co-located generation to pay a 
discounted NITS rate for transmission service. 
26. E3 proposes that the full NITS rate applies for firm interconnection 
service.  However, for the other service options, contingent and interruptible, 
E3 is proposing a discount from the full NITS rate, which seems to reflect an 
avoided cost concept. The calculation starts with use of the net present value 
of the ten-year Regional Transmission Expansion Plan (“RTEP”) incremental 
investment forecast. While PJM and every other RTO attempt to develop 
accurate forecasts, no RTO has come close to accurately forecasting 
transmission expansion costs and, in most cases to date, their forecasts have 
been substantially lower than their observed actuals. 
 
6  
See Answer of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC, at Ex. 2, Testimony of Zachary Ming, at 9:14–15.

12 
27. E3 then proposes to assume that only 50% of the projected incremental 
investment is due to load growth, so the projected marginal cost used in 
calculating the rate discount is only half of the projected incremental 
investment.  No basis is given for the use of 50%, and while some other 
percentage could be used, any such number would be pure speculation over a 
ten-year forecast period. Using E3’s example numbers, the NITS rate is 
$63/kW-year while the incremental investment (without the 50% load 
growth discount) is $52/kW-year. The 50% reduction brings this to $26/kW-
year, which is how E3 generates what they refer to as a 41% discount factor to 
be applied to the NITS rate. None of these numbers has any basis in fact, and 
ultimately there is no basis in using this discount or any other discount for “as 
available” or interruptible transmission service. Use of the transmission 
system to deliver power is a use of the system, regardless of whether that use 
is firm, contingent, or interruptible.7 
28. E3 applies the “as-available” concept only to its proposed interconnection 
arrangements. The “as-available” concept depends on the idea that “as-
available” energy purchases do not impose any costs on the transmission 
system while at the same time, as stated in the Ming testimony, “withdrawing 
energy from the transmission system clearly reflects a ‘use’ of the transmission 
system.”8 Setting aside an analysis of the methodology employed by E3, the 
 
7  
See Answer of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC, at Ex. 2, Testimony of Zachary Ming, at 38:1–39:12. 
8  
See Answer of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC, at Ex. 2, Testimony of Zachary Ming, at 37:9–16.

13 
concept of “use” proposed by E3, which is the basis of the development of the 
“as-available” charge, is predicated on the novel idea that a charge 
representing a service for which there is supposedly no incremental cost 
should be developed on a discounted basis and applied to a limited number of 
customers. This disparate treatment of customer classes is unduly 
discriminatory.  
29. The discriminatory nature of this proposal is apparent when considering 
otherwise similarly situated loads. For example, a ski resort operates only in 
winter and runs its snow guns at night. A large greenhouse also operates its 
lighting at night. Even though these transmission customers may or may not 
be firm loads, they pay the same NITS rate for transmission service that is paid 
by a large high load factor industrial load. However, these customers likely pay 
only de minimis transmission charges because most of their load occurs 
during off peak times. They do not impose incremental load on the 
transmission system and they pay the full NITS rate for whatever transmission 
service they do use, but because transmission charges are allocated based on 
contribution to coincident peak, their charges are minimized.  No additional 
rate discount is needed or applied. The fact that a data center with co-located 
generation is much larger is irrelevant to the discussion of discrimination, and 
discounted NITS rates for co-location are inappropriate and unduly 
discriminatory.

14 
V. 
Price Signals through NITS Are Neither Appropriate Nor Required to Incent 
Economically Efficient Siting Decisions. 
A. Bonbright Rate Design Principles Do Not Support Price Signaling for Specific 
Commercial Arrangements. 
30. E3 contends that the proposed rate designs are consistent with the Bonbright 
principles and are therefore just and reasonable. However, the use of price 
signals—specifically, a discounted transmission rate—to facilitate commercial 
arrangements such as a co-located business model is not among Bonbright’s 
criteria for sound rate design. 
31. As explained previously, offering a discounted rate to co-located load while 
requiring other load customers to pay the full transmission rate contravenes 
the Bonbright principle of Fairness in Cost Allocation, which holds that costs 
should be allocated equitably and without undue discrimination among 
customer classes or individuals.  
32. E3’s proposal to send price signals to facilitate the co-located business model 
alone, while charging undiscounted rates to all other customer classes, is 
misaligned with sound rate design principles. Indeed, if some customers pay 
discounted rates, other customers will have to make up that slack (the amount 
not paid on account of the discounts) by paying a yet higher rate. The Indicated 
PJM Transmission Owners have previously documented, in this proceeding, 
the material existence of unduly discriminatory cost shifting that would attend 
to such proposals.9 It is not sound rate design to give one group of customers a 
discount and charge a disproportionately high rate to all other customers, even 
 
9  
See Answer of the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners at 19 (Mar. 24, 2025).

15 
though many customers might be able to make a claim that their incremental system 
usage, by some metric, is lower than average.  
B. Transmission Rates Differ Fundamentally from PJM’s LMPs. 
33. E3 attempts to justify its price signal rationale by drawing a parallel to PJM’s 
energy market.10 However, this comparison is flawed—PJM’s energy market is 
in a competitive framework, whereas transmission is part of a regulated utility 
framework. Applying market-based pricing logic to the pricing framework of a 
regulated transmission system misconstrues the role and purpose of transmission 
rates.  
34.  Among other things, the LMP energy market sends short-term price signals that 
allow market participants to rapidly respond to the changing need for energy. The 
transmission grid, however, is a fixed investment in both the short-term and 
intermediate-term. When one customer avoids the cost of the transmission grid, it 
falls to another to pay it.    
C. Load Entities Already Have Strong Financial Incentives to Minimize Total 
Costs 
35. E3 contends that without a transmission discount, load has no incentive to co-
locate with generation. This is incorrect: load entities seeking interconnection 
already face strong financial drivers to minimize overall costs, including those 
associated with transmission upgrades, transmission charges, and energy 
procurement. Co-location often requires fewer transmission upgrades and 
reduces energy costs due to lower congestion and losses.   
 
10  Answer of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC, Ex. 2, Testimony of Zachary Ming, at 23 (Apr. 23, 2025).

16 
36. Additionally, data center siting decisions include the consideration of other 
significant factors such as climate conditions, tax and regulatory incentives, 
fiber-optic infrastructure, and security. All transmission customers would like 
to pay less for their service, but billions of dollars are going to be spent on data 
centers, and the data centers face a broad array of cost drivers. There is no 
reason to believe that transmission discounts are even a primary driver in that 
cost portfolio. 
D. Transmission Rates Are Not the Primary Driver of Co-location Decisions. 
37. As noted by the Data Center Coalition, the main motivation for co-location is 
access to timely interconnection, not transmission costs. Their statement 
reads: “co-location of load with generation—whether front-of-the-meter or 
behind-the-meter—is a pragmatic, common, and commercially legitimate 
strategy to secure timely access to power as markets grapple with years-long 
interconnection 
queue 
backlogs.”11 
In 
short, 
speed-to-power, 
not 
transmission pricing, is the decisive factor when large load seeks to co-locate 
with generation. E3’s price signaling through a discounted transmission rate 
is unnecessary given existing economic incentives and market behavior for co-
location decisions. 
VI. 
Conclusion 
38. The E3 Proposal put forth by Mr. Ming is untenable. It is premised on a flexible 
interconnection framework that does not currently exist and is not applicable 
 
11  Comments of the Data Center Coalition at 2 (Apr. 23, 2025).

17 
to the issue at hand. It fails to consider significant reliability and safety 
concerns presented by the interconnection of large loads such as data centers. 
These concerns are still being studied. It inappropriately utilizes a marginal 
cost discount in the design of transmission rates for certain customers only, 
an approach that is unwarranted and unduly discriminatory. Finally, it relies 
on an application of rate design principles that is flawed and fails to consider 
the primary motivation of co-location decisions (i.e., the ability to interconnect 
quickly).

VERIFICATION 
 
I declare under penalty of perjury that the foregoing Declaration is true and correct 
to the best of my information, knowledge, and belief. 
Executed this 3rd day of June 2025.
